definition: An ordinary file whose contents are just a sequence of bytes the operating system doesn't interpret, as opposed to special files such as directories, devices, pipes and sockets.
example: A JPEG photo and a SQLite database are both regular files.

definition: A special file that maps names to files (on Unix, to inode numbers). Directories inside directories form the file tree rooted at /.
example: /home/alfie is a directory containing entries such as notes.txt.

definition: A string naming a file by the route through the directory tree, with components separated by /. The kernel walks it one component at a time.
example: /home/alfie/notes.txt has three components: home, alfie and notes.txt.

definition: A path that starts with /, so it is resolved from the root directory regardless of where the process currently is.
example: /etc/hosts means the same file to every process with the same root.

definition: A path that does not start with /, so it is resolved from the process's current working directory (or from a supplied directory descriptor in calls such as openat).
example: From /home/alfie, ../docs/a.md means /home/docs/a.md.

definition: The top of the directory tree, written /. On ext4 its inode number is always 2.
example: Every absolute path is resolved starting from the root directory.

definition: A directory where another file system is attached into the tree, so its files appear underneath that directory.
example: Mounting a USB stick at /mnt/usb makes its files appear as /mnt/usb/...

definition: A Linux feature giving a group of processes its own view of which file systems are mounted where. Containers use it so they see a different file tree from the host.
example: A container can see its own / even though the host's / is a different disk.

definition: Universal Serial Bus, the common connector and protocol for plugging peripherals such as storage sticks, keyboards and external disks into a computer.
example: A USB stick is usually formatted with FAT32 or exFAT so every OS can read it.

definition: The system call that copies up to a requested number of bytes from an open file into a buffer and advances the offset. It can return fewer bytes than asked, and 0 at end of file.
example: read(fd, buf, 100) on a 7-byte file returns 7.

definition: The system call that copies bytes from a buffer to an open file, pipe or socket. For ordinary buffered files it returns once the data is in the page cache, not once it is on disk, and it can transfer fewer bytes than asked.
example: write(fd, b'hello', 5) normally returns 5 long before the bytes reach the disk.

definition: The system call that releases a file descriptor. It does not mean the data is on disk.
example: A server must close a descriptor per request, or it eventually hits the descriptor limit.

definition: The system call that moves an open file description's offset, to an absolute position, relative to the current one, or relative to the end (SEEK_SET, SEEK_CUR, SEEK_END).
example: lseek(fd, 0, SEEK_END) moves to the end of the file.

definition: An open flag that makes every write go to the current end of the file, with the seek and write done as one atomic step on a local file system. NFS cannot guarantee this across clients.
example: Two processes appending log lines with O_APPEND on ext4 never overwrite each other.

definition: The permission bits stored in a file's inode, usually written in octal: read (4), write (2) and execute (1) for the owner, the group and everyone else. 0644 means owner read/write, others read-only.
example: -rw-r--r-- is mode 644.

definition: Base-8 notation, using digits 0–7. Unix permissions are written in octal because each digit holds exactly three permission bits; Python writes octal literals with a 0o prefix.
A per-process mask of permission bits to remove from newly created files. A requested mode of 0644 with a umask of 022 stays 0644; with 077 it becomes 0600.
example: A typical umask of 022 stops new files being writable by group and others.

definition: Access control list: extra per-user or per-group permission entries on a file beyond the basic owner/group/other mode bits. A directory's default ACL is applied to files created inside it.
example: An ACL can grant bob read access to one file without changing its group.

definition: The x permission bit. On a file it allows running it; on a directory it means search permission, which is needed to look up any name inside it during path resolution.
example: Without x on /home/alice, bob cannot reach /home/alice/report.txt even if that file is world-readable.

definition: A file whose permission bits let every user read it (the 'others' read bit is set).
example: Mode 644 makes a file world-readable.

definition: Python's standard module exposing raw operating-system calls such as os.open, os.read, os.write and os.fsync, without the buffering the built-in open() adds.
example: os.write(fd, data) is a thin wrapper around the write system call.

definition: A Python object that gives a view onto another object's bytes without copying them, so slicing off the written part of a buffer is cheap.
example: view = view[n:] drops the first n bytes from the view without copying the rest.

definition: The number identifying an inode within one file system. Directory entries map names to inode numbers, which are only unique within a single file system.
example: On ext4 the root directory is always inode number 2.

definition: A command that reports free and used space on mounted file systems; df -i reports inodes instead of blocks.
example: df -h /var shows 40% used while df -i /var shows 100% of inodes used.

definition: A command that reports the disk space files actually occupy (allocated blocks), which can be much smaller than their size for sparse files.
example: du -h disk.img can show 0 for a 10 GiB sparse file.

definition: A tool that lists open files and the processes holding them. lsof +L1 lists files that are open but have no remaining names (link count below 1).
example: lsof +L1 finds the deleted 50 GB log that a process is still writing.

definition: The error 'Too many open files': the process has reached its limit on open file descriptors, usually because descriptors are leaking.
example: A server that never closes client sockets eventually fails accept() with EMFILE.

definition: The error 'No space left on device': there are no free data blocks, or no free inodes, to satisfy the request.
example: Creating a file on a disk with free blocks but no free inodes fails with ENOSPC.

definition: The error 'Permission denied': the caller lacks a required permission, such as search permission on a directory in the path.
example: cat /home/alice/report.txt fails with EACCES if bob cannot search /home/alice.

definition: The error 'No such file or directory': a name in the path does not exist.
example: Removing a name that was already removed fails with ENOENT.

definition: The NFS error 'Stale file handle': the client used a file handle that no longer identifies a valid object on the server, for example after the file was deleted there.
example: An NFS client with a cached handle to a file another client deleted can get ESTALE.

definition: The record describing a whole file system: its block size, how many inodes and blocks it has, where its tables are, and a magic number identifying its type. In the VFS, a superblock object represents one mounted file system.
example: ext4 stores backup copies of its superblock in several block groups.

definition: A C struct whose fields are pointers to functions. Each file system fills in tables such as file_operations and inode_operations, and the VFS calls through them: a C form of interface-based polymorphism.
example: ext4's file_operations.read_iter points at ext4's own read code.

definition: The kernel's walk through a path one component at a time, looking each name up in the current directory and checking search permission, until it reaches the target's inode.
example: Resolving /home/alfie/notes.txt looks up home, then alfie, then notes.txt.

definition: ext4's predecessors. ext2 (1993) had no journal; ext3 (2001) added one. Both map file data with 12 direct pointers plus single-, double- and triple-indirect blocks.
example: An ext3 file of 1 GiB needs about 1 MiB of indirect blocks.

definition: A high-performance journaling file system designed by SGI, now common on Linux servers. It splits the disk into allocation groups and uses B+ trees for free space and inodes.
example: XFS can grow online, but shrink support is limited.

definition: A copy-on-write Linux file system with checksums, snapshots, subvolumes, compression and built-in RAID profiles.
example: openSUSE uses Btrfs snapshots to roll back a failed upgrade.

definition: File Allocation Table, the MS-DOS file system family. A table at the start of the disk holds one next-cluster entry per cluster, so each file is a linked chain of clusters.
example: A USB stick is often FAT32 because nearly every device can read it.

definition: The 32-bit FAT variant. Its file-size field limits a single file to 4 GiB minus one byte, and it has no Unix-style permissions or journal.
example: A 5 GB video cannot be copied onto a FAT32 stick as one file.

definition: Extended FAT, Microsoft's successor to FAT32 for flash media, without the 4 GiB file-size limit.
example: SDXC cards are formatted exFAT by default.

definition: A special file under /dev that represents a device driver, so programs can use open, read and write on hardware.
example: /dev/sda is a whole disk; /dev/null discards writes.

definition: A device file that discards everything written to it and always reports end of file when read.
example: command > /dev/null throws away the command's output.

definition: A device file that produces cryptographically secure random bytes from the kernel's random number generator.
example: head -c 8 /dev/urandom prints eight random bytes.

definition: A Linux socket family used to configure kernel networking, such as interfaces and routes, from user space.
example: The ip command configures eth0 over netlink.

definition: The signalling speed of a serial line, in symbols per second.
example: An old serial terminal might run at 9,600 baud.

definition: A research operating system from Bell Labs, the successor to Unix, that pushed 'everything is a file' much further, even representing network connections and windows as files.
example: In Plan 9 a network connection is opened by writing to files under /net.

definition: The Unix design idea that one interface (open, read, write, close on file descriptors) works for files, devices, pipes, sockets and kernel state.
example: cat works on /proc/loadavg just as on a text file.

definition: The library for Linux's older native asynchronous I/O interface (io_submit), mainly useful with O_DIRECT.
example: Benchmarks such as fio can use libaio to keep many direct reads in flight.

definition: The fixed-size unit a storage device or file system reads, writes and allocates, typically 4 KiB in a file system. In NAND flash, 'block' also names the larger erase unit, a group of pages that must be erased together.
example: A 1-byte file on ext4 still occupies one whole 4 KiB block.

definition: The smallest unit a disk addresses: traditionally 512 bytes, 4 KiB on many modern drives. The logical sector size the drive reports can be smaller than its physical sector size.
example: A 512e drive reports 512-byte logical sectors but writes 4 KiB physical sectors.

definition: Terabyte: 10^12 bytes in decimal units, the way drive capacities are sold.
example: A 16 TB disk holds 1.28 × 10^14 bits.

definition: Gigabits per second, a link speed of 10^9 bits per second. Divide by 8 for bytes, before protocol overhead.
example: SATA's 6 Gb/s link carries at most about 600 MB/s of data.

definition: Data or free space broken into many scattered pieces. For files, it means a file's data lies in many separate runs on the device instead of a few long ones, making sequential reads slower on disks and needing more mapping metadata; in memory, it means free space split into gaps too small to use.
example: Random updates on a copy-on-write file system can fragment a database file into thousands of extents.

definition: An array with one bit per object recording whether it is free or in use. File systems keep one for inodes and one for data blocks.
example: A 4 KiB block bitmap tracks 32,768 blocks.

definition: A fixed array of inodes laid out on disk, created by mkfs. In ext4 each block group has its own, so the number of inodes is fixed for a given file system size.
example: Running out of inode-table slots stops file creation even with free blocks.

definition: A block holding file contents or directory contents, as opposed to metadata such as inodes and bitmaps.
example: Appending to a file allocates a new data block and updates the inode to point at it.

definition: A fixed value stored at a known place in a structure so software can recognise what it is.
example: The ext4 superblock contains the magic number 0xEF53.

definition: The command that creates (formats) a file system on a device, laying out the superblock, bitmaps and inode tables. mke2fs is ext2/3/4's version.
example: mkfs.ext4 -i 4096 creates more inodes for a disk full of tiny files.

definition: A slice of an ext2/3/4 file system with its own bitmaps and inode table, so a file's inode and data can be kept close together. With 4 KiB blocks and one-block bitmaps a group spans 128 MiB.
example: A 1 TiB ext4 file system has about 8,192 block groups.

definition: ext4 format features that change the classic layout: flex_bg packs several groups' metadata together, meta_bg changes where group descriptors live, and bigalloc allocates in clusters of several blocks.
example: bigalloc with 64 KiB clusters reduces allocation metadata for huge files.

definition: User ID and group ID: the numbers the kernel uses for a file's owner and group.
example: uid 1000 is usually the first ordinary user on a Linux system.

definition: A file's three classic timestamps: atime (last access), mtime (last modification of the contents) and ctime (last change to the inode, such as permissions).
example: chmod changes ctime but not mtime.

definition: A mount option that stops reads from updating atime, avoiding a metadata write on every read. relatime, the Linux default, updates it only occasionally.
example: Mounting a busy mail spool with noatime removes many small writes.

definition: Running out of free inodes while data blocks remain free, so new files cannot be created; df -i shows it.
example: Millions of tiny cache files can exhaust inodes with the disk only 40% full.

definition: The directory where JavaScript's npm installs a project's dependencies, often containing tens of thousands of small files.
example: A few node_modules trees can consume hundreds of thousands of inodes.

definition: ext4's hashed directory index: a shallow B-tree-like structure keyed on a hash of each name, so lookups in huge directories take about O(log n) steps instead of scanning every entry.
example: A directory with 100,000 entries can be searched in a few block reads with htree.

definition: An additional directory entry pointing at the same inode. All names are equal peers; the file survives until the last name is removed. Hard links cannot cross file systems or (normally) point at directories.
example: ln a b makes b a second name for a's inode.

definition: A symbolic link whose target path no longer exists, so following it fails.
example: After rm a, a symlink c → a dangles until a new a is created.

definition: The number of directory entries (names) pointing at an inode, stored in the inode. A file's storage can be freed only when it reaches zero and no process still has it open.
example: Two hard links give a file link count 2.

definition: The command that creates links: ln a b makes a hard link, ln -s a c makes a symbolic link.
example: ln -s /data/current latest creates a symlink called latest.

definition: An ext4 feature that lets a directory have more than about 65,000 subdirectories, by reporting a link count of 1 to mean 'unknown' once the count would overflow.
example: With dir_nlink, a directory with 70,000 subdirectories shows link count 1.

definition: A symbolic link whose target is short enough (under 60 bytes on ext4) to be stored inside the inode itself, so following it needs no extra block read.
example: ln -s ../lib lib on ext4 creates a fast symlink.

definition: Storing each file in one run of consecutive blocks, so the inode needs only a start and a length. Simple and fast to read, but files can't grow easily and free space fragments.
example: ISO 9660 CDs use contiguous allocation because files are written once.

definition: Storing a file as a chain of blocks where each block (or a table entry, as in FAT) points to the next. Appending is easy but reaching a far position means following the chain.
example: Reaching cluster 1,000 of a FAT file means following 999 table entries.

definition: In FAT (and ext4 bigalloc), the allocation unit: a group of consecutive sectors or blocks treated as one.
example: A FAT32 volume with 32 KiB clusters gives every small file at least 32 KiB.

definition: The standard file system for CD-ROMs, which stores files contiguously because the disc is written once.
example: Linux install images are ISO 9660 file systems.

definition: Microsoft's disk operating system for IBM PCs, from 1981, which introduced FAT to most users.
example: Floppy disks formatted under MS-DOS used FAT12.

definition: Keeping an array of pointers to a file's blocks in its inode, with indirect blocks for larger files, so any block can be found by arithmetic plus a few reads.
example: ext2/3 use indexed allocation with 15 pointers in each inode.

definition: A number stored in an inode or indirect block giving the address of a data block (or of another pointer block). ext2/3 use 4-byte (32-bit) block pointers.
example: With 4 KiB blocks, one indirect block holds 1,024 four-byte pointers.

definition: A block pointer stored in the inode itself that points straight at a data block. ext2/3 inodes have 12, covering the first 48 KiB with 4 KiB blocks.
example: Reading a 10 KiB file needs only its direct pointers.

definition: A block filled with block pointers rather than data. A single-indirect pointer leads to one such block; double- and triple-indirect pointers add one or two more levels, each multiplying the number of reachable blocks.
example: With 4 KiB blocks the double-indirect level reaches 1,048,576 blocks, 4 GiB.

definition: A single record mapping a run of consecutive file blocks onto consecutive device blocks: logical start, length and physical start. In ext4 each takes 12 bytes and covers up to 32,768 blocks.
example: One extent can say 'file blocks 0–2,999 are at disk blocks 81,920–84,919'.

definition: The shallow B-tree ext4 builds when a file has more extents than fit in its inode (four): index nodes point down to leaf blocks full of extents.
example: A 10 GiB contiguous file needs 80 extents, held in a depth-1 extent tree.

definition: The 60-byte area in an ext4 inode that holds either the 15 classic block pointers or an extent header plus four extent entries (or a fast symlink's target).
example: An inode's i_block fits a 12-byte header and four 12-byte extents.

definition: Choosing disk blocks when dirty data is written back rather than at write() time, so the allocator sees more of the file at once and can choose long contiguous runs.
example: ext4's delayed allocation lets a 100 MB file written in small pieces land in a few large extents.

definition: Allocating many blocks in one request instead of one at a time, which helps produce long extents.
example: ext4's mballoc allocator reserves a whole run for a large write-back.

definition: Reserving space for a file in advance, for example with fallocate, so later writes won't fail for lack of space and can land in a better layout. It does not guarantee physical contiguity.
example: fallocate -l 10G db.img reserves 10 GiB before the database starts writing.

definition: A file with holes: ranges that were never written and have no blocks allocated, which read back as zeros. Its logical size can be far larger than its disk usage.
example: truncate -s 10G disk.img creates a 10 GiB file that uses almost no space.

definition: A range of a sparse file with no allocated blocks. Reading it returns zeros without any disk I/O for that range.
example: A VM image with 44 GB of holes uses only 6 GB on disk.

definition: Setting a file's length: cutting it shorter or extending it (with a hole) to a given size.
example: truncate -s 0 app.log empties a log in place.

definition: A file-copying tool that can copy efficiently over a network; rsync -S (--sparse) recreates holes instead of writing zeros.
example: rsync -S vm.img backup:/ keeps the copy sparse.

definition: lseek options that jump to the next hole or the next data region of a sparse file, so copy tools can skip holes without reading them.
example: cp --sparse uses SEEK_DATA to find the allocated ranges.

definition: A file holding the entire virtual disk of a virtual machine, usually sparse so unused space takes nothing on the host.
example: A 50 GB VM image may occupy only 6 GB of real space.

definition: The problem of keeping on-disk structures valid when power fails part-way through an update that needs several block writes, since any subset of those writes may have reached the disk.
example: Appending one block needs the data block, inode and bitmap updated; a crash can persist any of them alone.

definition: File system check: a tool run after a crash that scans all metadata, rebuilds bitmaps, fixes link counts and moves orphaned inodes to lost+found. It restores consistency, not correct contents, and its time grows with the file system's size. e2fsck is ext2/3/4's version.
example: A full fsck of a multi-terabyte array of hard disks can take hours.

definition: A directory at the root of an ext file system where fsck places orphaned files that are in use but have no name in any directory.
example: After a bad crash, fsck may leave files named #12345 in lost+found.

definition: An inode that is marked in use but not referenced by any directory entry, typically left behind by a crash.
example: fsck reconnects orphaned inodes into lost+found.

definition: A block the bitmap marks as used although no inode points at it, so its space is lost until a checker reclaims it.
example: A crash after writing only the bitmap leaks one block.

definition: Writing a description of each update to a reserved on-disk log, the journal, before changing the real structures in place, so after a crash the update can be replayed or discarded instead of scanning the whole disk. It is file-system write-ahead logging.
example: ext4 journals metadata changes and replays committed ones at mount after a crash.

definition: One atomic group of logged changes in a journal: a begin block (TxB), copies of the changed blocks, then a commit block (TxE). Only transactions with a valid commit block are replayed after a crash.
example: A transaction found with TxB but no TxE is discarded on recovery.

definition: The step that makes a transaction count: writing the commit record (TxE) after everything it covers is on disk. Before the commit, recovery discards the transaction; after it, recovery replays it.
example: ext4 commits a journal transaction every 5 seconds by default.

definition: In journaling, writing committed blocks to their real locations so the journal space can be freed. In LFS, a fixed on-disk record pointing at the latest inode-map pieces. In a database such as PostgreSQL, the checkpointer flushes dirty pages so old log can be recycled.
example: After checkpointing, the journal space for that transaction is marked free.

definition: Re-applying committed log records after a crash so the on-disk structures reach the state the log describes. Replaying the same transaction twice is harmless.
example: At mount, ext4 replays every committed transaction still in the journal.

definition: Journaling Block Device 2: the Linux kernel layer that implements ext4's journal.
example: ext4's jbd2 thread commits transactions in the background.

definition: The ext4 mode that journals file data as well as metadata, so every data byte is written twice: once to the journal, once to its home location.
example: Streaming 1 GB in data=journal mode writes about 2 GB.

definition: ext4's default journaling mode: only metadata is journaled, but data blocks are written to their final location before the metadata that points at them commits, so after a crash newly allocated blocks do not expose stale old contents.
example: A file extended in ordered mode never grows over unwritten garbage.

definition: An ext4 journaling mode that journals metadata only with no ordering for data, so after a crash a file can show stale old contents from previously deleted files.
example: data=writeback is faster but can expose another file's old data after a crash.

definition: A setting chosen when a file system is mounted, such as data=ordered, commit=5 or noatime.
example: mount -o noatime,commit=15 /dev/sda1 /data sets two mount options.

definition: The ext4 mount option giving how often (in seconds) the journal commits a transaction; the default is 5. It schedules commits and is not a promise about how much data a crash can lose.
example: commit=15 batches journal commits every 15 seconds.

definition: ext4 journal options. journal_checksum adds checksums to journal transactions so incomplete ones can be detected; journal_async_commit uses them to write the commit block without first waiting for the other blocks. They are distinct settings.
example: With journal checksums, a commit block written before its data is recognised as invalid.

definition: Never overwriting live data: a change is written to a new location and then the pointer to it is updated, all the way up to a new root. A crash before the root switch leaves the old version intact. Also used for memory pages after fork.
example: Btrfs and ZFS are copy-on-write file systems.

definition: ZFS's root record identifying the latest committed tree. ZFS keeps an array of checksummed uberblocks and at import picks the newest valid one.
example: A crash before a new uberblock is written leaves the previous tree as the live one.

definition: A read-only, point-in-time view of a file system or volume. On copy-on-write systems it initially shares all blocks with the live data and only consumes space as data changes.
example: A Btrfs snapshot before an upgrade lets you roll back if it fails.

definition: Data that changes on the storage medium or along the I/O path without any error being reported, so it is returned as if valid unless something checks a checksum.
example: A flipped bit in a photo on an unchecked file system goes unnoticed until the photo is opened.

definition: A Btrfs attribute (set with chattr +C on an empty file or a directory) that makes files be overwritten in place instead of copy-on-write. It also disables data checksums and compression for those files.
example: Databases on Btrfs are often placed in a chattr +C directory to limit fragmentation.

definition: A Linux command that sets file attributes such as immutable or, on Btrfs, NOCOW (+C).
example: chattr +C /var/lib/mysql makes new files there NOCOW.

definition: How many bytes are physically written for each byte the application or host asked to write. Copy-on-write paths, journaling and SSD garbage collection all raise it; 1 is ideal.
example: An SSD cleaning blocks that are 75% valid has write amplification of about 4.

definition: The ZFS Intent Log: a log of synchronous operations that lets fsync return without waiting for the next full transaction group. It is replayed after a crash and lives in the pool unless a separate log device is added.
example: An NFS server's synchronous writes go to the ZIL first.

definition: Btrfs's log for fast fsync: it records recent changes so fsync need not commit a whole transaction, and is replayed at mount after a crash.
example: fsync on Btrfs usually writes the tree log rather than a full commit.

definition: Like fsync, but it may skip metadata not needed to read the data back, such as the modification time.
example: A log writer can use fdatasync after appending, since the file size change is still flushed.

definition: Storage whose contents survive power loss, such as the magnetic platter or NAND cells, as opposed to volatile caches in RAM.
example: Data in a drive's volatile cache has not yet reached stable storage.

definition: The system call that changes a file's name, replacing any existing file at the target. Within one file system it is atomic: other processes see the old file or the new one, never a mix.
example: Writing config.tmp then renaming it over config.json updates the file atomically.

definition: A function that creates and opens a new temporary file with a unique name and owner-only permissions (0600).
example: tempfile.mkstemp(dir='.') returns a descriptor and a path such as ./tmpa1b2c3.

definition: An ext4 heuristic, on by default, that detects replace-via-rename and replace-via-truncate patterns and forces the new data out before the rename commits, limiting zero-length files after crashes.
example: auto_da_alloc was added after ext4's 2009 zero-length-file reports.

definition: The 2018 discovery, reported by Craig Ringer, that PostgreSQL could lose data on Linux because a failed fsync could mark unwritten pages clean, so retrying fsync later reported success.
example: After fsyncgate, PostgreSQL 11.2 started to PANIC on data-file fsync failure.

definition: Presenting a volume larger than the physical space behind it, allocating real space only when data is written. If the pool runs out, writes fail with I/O errors.
example: A thin-provisioned 1 TB volume backed by 500 GB fails writes once the 500 GB is used.

definition: The Linux 4.13 mechanism for tracking write-back errors per file with a sequence counter, so each open file description can see an error recorded since it last checked.
example: With errseq_t, two processes that both call fsync can each learn of a write-back error.

definition: PostgreSQL's most severe error level: the server stops all sessions and restarts, recovering from its write-ahead log. Since 11.2 it PANICs on data-file fsync failure by default, controlled by data_sync_retry.
example: An fsync EIO on a data file now makes PostgreSQL PANIC and replay its WAL.

definition: Storage area network: a dedicated network giving servers block-level access to shared storage arrays.
example: A transient SAN fault can make an fsync fail with EIO.

definition: RAM inside a drive or controller that holds written data before it reaches the medium. Its contents are lost on power failure unless flushed or protected.
example: A drive may acknowledge a write as soon as it lands in its volatile write cache.

definition: A command telling a drive to write everything in its volatile write cache to stable media before reporting completion. File systems issue it to make journal commits durable.
example: fsync ends with a cache flush to the device.

definition: Force Unit Access: a flag on a write telling the drive to put that write on stable media before completing it, bypassing its volatile cache for that write.
example: ext4 can write the journal commit block with FUA.

definition: Capacitors or batteries in a drive or controller that supply enough energy, on power failure, to write cached data to stable media.
example: An SSD with power-loss protection can safely complete flushes quickly.

definition: The 2009 ext4 issue where, after crashes, applications that replaced files via rename without fsync found them empty, because delayed allocation let the rename commit before the data was written.
example: A config file saved just before a crash could come back 0 bytes long.

definition: In NAND flash, the unit that is read or programmed, often 16 KiB; many pages make up one erase block. (A memory page is a different, though similarly named, unit.)
example: A 4 MiB erase block might hold 256 flash pages of 16 KiB.

definition: A Linux kernel structure representing a power-of-two group of contiguous memory pages managed as one unit, so the page cache can handle large files with less overhead.
example: A 2 MiB folio stands for 512 contiguous 4 KiB pages.

definition: A lookup that finds the wanted data already in the cache, so no slower storage access is needed.
example: Reading a page that is already in the page cache is a cache hit: just a memory copy.

definition: A Linux control file: writing 3 to it discards clean page-cache, dentry and inode cache contents, used to test cold-cache performance. It does not write dirty data, so run sync first.
example: sync; echo 3 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches empties the clean caches on a test box.

definition: Kernel threads that write dirty pages back to storage in the background, waking periodically and when dirty data passes a threshold.
example: With dirty_writeback_centisecs = 500 the flusher wakes every 5 seconds.

definition: One hundredth of a second (0.01 s). Some Linux write-back settings use it as their unit.
example: 3000 centiseconds is 30 seconds.

definition: How old dirty data must be, in centiseconds, before periodic write-back picks it up; commonly 3000 (30 s). It is an eligibility threshold, not a durability deadline.
example: With 3000, a page dirtied at 12:00:00 becomes eligible at 12:00:30.

definition: How often, in centiseconds, the flusher threads wake to write back old dirty data; commonly 500 (5 s).
example: Setting it to 100 makes the flusher wake every second.

definition: The percentage of dirtyable memory (or, with dirty_background_bytes, a fixed byte count) at which background write-back starts. Setting the bytes version disables the ratio.
example: With 10% of 64 GiB, background flushing starts at 6.4 GiB of dirty data.

definition: The percentage of dirtyable memory (or, with dirty_bytes, a fixed byte count) at which write throttling starts: processes doing writes are made to wait for write-back.
example: With dirty_ratio 20 and 64 GiB dirtyable, writers stall at about 12.8 GiB dirty.

definition: The kernel's count of memory that may hold dirty page-cache data, roughly free plus reclaimable memory with some exclusions. The dirty ratios are percentages of this, not of installed RAM.
example: A 64 GiB machine may have noticeably less than 64 GiB dirtyable.

definition: The kernel deliberately slowing a process that writes, making it sleep while write-back catches up, once too much dirty data has built up (around dirty_ratio).
example: Once dirty_ratio is reached, write throttling holds cp to the USB disk's 30 MB/s.

definition: Detaching a mounted file system. umount first writes back all its dirty data, so it can wait a long time on a slow device.
example: umount /mnt/usb can take minutes after a big copy to a slow stick.

definition: The command and system call that write all dirty data to storage. POSIX only requires sync() to schedule the writes, but on Linux it waits for them to complete.
example: Run sync before pulling power from a test machine.

definition: Open flags that make each write wait for storage: it returns only once the data (O_DSYNC) or data plus metadata (O_SYNC) is on stable storage, like an fsync after every write.
example: A log opened with O_DSYNC needs no separate fdatasync call.

definition: Caching the same data twice, once in an application's own cache and again in the kernel's page cache, wasting memory and adding a copy.
example: InnoDB with buffered I/O can hold the same 16 KiB page in its buffer pool and the page cache.

definition: A high-performance distributed NoSQL database, compatible with Cassandra, that manages its own memory and uses direct I/O.
example: ScyllaDB bypasses the page cache and caches rows itself.

definition: Oracle Corporation's commercial relational database, which manages its own buffer cache and commonly uses direct I/O.
example: Oracle Database's buffer cache plays the role of InnoDB's buffer pool.

definition: PostgreSQL's setting for the size of its own page cache. Because PostgreSQL also relies on the OS page cache, about 25% of RAM is the usual starting point on a dedicated server.
example: On a 64 GiB server, shared_buffers might start at 16 GiB.

definition: A statx request that asks the kernel for a file's direct-I/O alignment requirements for memory buffers and file offsets, where supported.
example: statx with STATX_DIOALIGN can report a 512-byte offset alignment.

definition: Direct Access: a Linux mode for persistent-memory devices where file data is mapped straight into memory without the page cache.
example: A file system on persistent memory mounted with -o dax bypasses the page cache.

definition: C functions for jumping out of a signal handler back to a saved point in the program, one awkward way to recover from SIGBUS.
example: An mmap-based reader may wrap accesses in sigsetjmp so a SIGBUS handler can siglongjmp out.

definition: Database management system: the software that stores, queries and manages a database, such as PostgreSQL or MySQL.
example: The CIDR 2022 paper argues against using mmap inside a DBMS.

definition: The Conference on Innovative Data Systems Research, a database research conference; not to be confused with CIDR address blocks in networking.
example: 'Are You Sure You Want to Use MMAP in Your DBMS?' appeared at CIDR 2022.

definition: A document-oriented NoSQL database. Its original MMAPv1 storage engine used mmap and was later replaced by WiredTiger.
example: MongoDB moved from MMAPv1 to WiredTiger as its default engine in version 3.2.

definition: DMA that reads from (or writes to) a list of separate memory areas in one operation, so data need not first be copied into one contiguous buffer.
example: A NIC with scatter-gather can transmit a packet's header and payload from different pages.

definition: Kernel memory holding data queued for sending (or received) on a socket.
example: send copies data from the program into the socket buffer before the NIC transmits it.

definition: Kernel TLS: a Linux feature that performs TLS record encryption in the kernel (or on the NIC), so encrypted connections can still use sendfile.
example: With kTLS, nginx can serve HTTPS files with sendfile.

definition: One server in a content delivery network that caches and serves content close to users.
example: A video CDN node serves the same popular files to thousands of viewers.

definition: The package of Linux process and memory utilities, including free, ps and top.
example: Column names in free differ between procps versions.

definition: Filling a cache with data that won't be reused, evicting data that would have been, such as a one-pass backup scan.
example: Reading a terabyte once through the page cache pollutes it.

definition: Hard disk drive: storage that records data magnetically on spinning platters, read and written by heads on a moving arm. Random access is slow (milliseconds) because the head must move and wait for the platter.
example: A 7,200 rpm HDD manages roughly 80–150 random reads per second.

definition: A rigid magnetic-coated disc inside a hard disk on which data is recorded; drives hold several on one spindle.
example: A 16 TB drive might have nine platters.

definition: The tiny sensor on a hard disk's arm that reads and writes magnetic data, flying just above the platter surface; there is one per surface.
example: Moving the head to a new track is the seek.

definition: The pivoting arm that positions a hard disk's heads over the right track.
example: The actuator arm moves all heads together.

definition: The motor-driven shaft that spins a hard disk's platters at a fixed speed.
example: The spindle of a 7,200 rpm drive turns 120 times a second.

definition: One concentric ring of data on a platter surface; each track is divided into sectors.
example: Reading sequentially along a track needs no seeks.

definition: The time a hard disk takes to move its heads to the right track, typically a few milliseconds and dependent on distance. (lseek, by contrast, just moves a file offset and costs no seek.)
example: An 8 ms average seek limits a disk to about 125 seeks per second.

definition: The time spent waiting for the wanted sector to rotate under the head; on average half a revolution.
example: At 7,200 rpm the average rotational latency is about 4.17 ms.

definition: The time to actually read or write the data once the head is in position; for a 4 KiB request on a disk streaming 200 MB/s, about 0.02 ms.
example: For random 4 KiB reads, transfer time is tiny next to seek and rotation.

definition: Revolutions per minute, the spin speed of a hard disk. One revolution takes 60 / rpm seconds.
example: A 15,000 rpm drive turns once every 4 ms.

definition: I/O operations per second: how many separate reads or writes a device or array completes each second, usually quoted for small random requests.
example: A queue-depth-one hard disk doing 12 ms random reads manages about 80 IOPS.

definition: The number of I/O requests outstanding at a device at once. Higher depths let devices work in parallel and reorder requests.
example: At queue depth 1, a disk handles one request at a time.

definition: Random I/O touches scattered locations; sequential I/O reads or writes consecutive locations in order. On hard disks sequential access is hundreds of times faster because it avoids seeks.
example: Reading a file front to back is sequential I/O.

definition: Kernel code that orders and merges block requests before sending them to a device. On hard disks it sorts by position to cut seeks; fast NVMe devices often use 'none'.
example: cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/scheduler might print [none] mq-deadline.

definition: A hard disk with 4 KiB physical sectors that presents 512-byte logical sectors for compatibility. Writes that are not 4 KiB-aligned force a read-modify-write inside the drive.
example: A partition starting at sector 63 on a 512e drive makes every 4 KiB write misaligned.

definition: Shingled magnetic recording: hard disks whose tracks overlap like roof tiles to fit more data, so rewriting one track disturbs its neighbours. Random writes become very slow once the drive's cache region fills.
example: A drive-managed SMR disk can slow drastically during a RAID rebuild.

definition: The non-volatile memory used in SSDs and USB sticks. It stores bits as trapped charge, is read and programmed in pages, erased only in whole blocks, and wears out after a limited number of erase cycles.
example: An SSD stripes data across many NAND flash dies to go fast.

definition: One storage transistor in NAND flash. Storing more bits per cell (by distinguishing more charge levels) raises density but lowers speed and endurance.
example: A QLC cell distinguishes 16 charge levels to store 4 bits.

definition: Single-level cell flash: 1 bit per cell, the fastest and most durable kind. Many desktop and laptop SSDs run part of their flash in SLC mode as a fast write cache.
example: Writes land in the SLC cache first and are folded into TLC later.

definition: Multi-level cell flash, usually meaning 2 bits per cell.
example: MLC was common in SSDs before TLC took over.

definition: Triple-level cell flash: 3 bits per cell, the most common type in current desktop and laptop SSDs.
example: A TLC cell must distinguish 8 charge levels.

definition: Quad-level cell flash: 4 bits per cell, dense and cheap but slower to write and less durable.
example: QLC drives suit read-heavy archives better than busy databases.

definition: Writing data into erased NAND flash pages. A page can be programmed only after its block has been erased.
example: Changing one programmed page requires writing the new data to a different, erased page.

definition: Resetting a whole NAND flash block (many pages, often megabytes) so its pages can be programmed again. Erasing is slow and wears the cells.
example: A block of 256 × 16 KiB pages must be erased as one 4 MiB unit.

definition: Program/erase cycle: one round of programming and erasing a flash block. Each block survives a limited number before it wears out.
example: Wear levelling spreads P/E cycles evenly across blocks.

definition: Flash translation layer: the SSD firmware that makes flash look like a simple disk. It writes out of place, keeps a mapping from logical block addresses to physical pages, garbage-collects and levels wear.
example: When the host overwrites LBA 7, the FTL writes a new page and updates its map.

definition: Software built into a device that controls its hardware, such as an SSD's controller code.
example: An SSD firmware update can change its garbage-collection behaviour.

definition: The processor inside an SSD (or disk) that runs its firmware and manages the media, caches and host interface.
example: The controller hides flash erase rules behind a plain read/write interface.

definition: Logical block address: the number a host uses to name a block on a storage device, counting from 0. The device decides where it physically lives.
example: An SSD's FTL might map LBA 7 to block 52, page 3.

definition: Writing updated data to a fresh location instead of overwriting the old one, then updating a map and marking the old copy invalid. Flash requires it; log-structured and copy-on-write designs use it too.
example: An SSD rewriting LBA 7 puts the new data in the next free page.

definition: The FTL's table from logical block addresses to physical flash locations. A page-level table with 4-byte entries per 4 KiB needs about 1 GiB per TiB of flash.
example: The mapping table records that LBA 7 now lives in block 52, page 3.

definition: A flash page whose data has been superseded by a newer copy elsewhere; it wastes space until garbage collection erases its block.
example: Overwriting LBA 7 marks its old page invalid.

definition: Automatically reclaiming space that is no longer in use. In an SSD's FTL it means picking blocks with many invalid pages, copying their still-valid pages elsewhere and erasing them; in programming languages it means freeing memory no longer reachable by the program.
example: When free blocks run low, SSD garbage collection copies the live pages out of a mostly stale block and erases it.

definition: The block an SSD's garbage collector chooses to clean. The fewer valid pages it holds, the less copying the clean costs.
example: A victim block that is 75% valid gives write amplification of about 4.

definition: Spreading erase cycles evenly across all flash blocks, occasionally moving cold data, so no block wears out early.
example: Wear levelling moves a rarely changed file so its block can take its share of erases.

definition: An NVMe feature that lets a DRAM-less SSD borrow a small part of the host's RAM to cache its mapping table.
example: A DRAM-less NVMe drive might use 64 MiB of host memory buffer.

definition: Flash capacity kept hidden from the host as spare space, giving garbage collection room to work and lowering write amplification.
example: A drive with 1,024 GiB (about 1,100 GB) of flash sold as 1,000 GB keeps about 10% over-provisioning.

definition: A command by which the file system tells an SSD which LBAs no longer hold useful data, so garbage collection need not copy them. On Linux, run fstrim periodically or mount with discard.
example: Without TRIM, a deleted 10 GB file still looks live to the SSD.

definition: An SSD's sustained performance after it has been filled and written enough that garbage collection runs continuously, as opposed to its fresh-out-of-the-box speed.
example: An SSD rated at 500,000 write IOPS fresh might sustain far less in steady state.

definition: The sudden drop in an SSD's write throughput, with latency spikes, once free blocks or its SLC cache run out and garbage collection competes with host writes.
example: A long random-write benchmark can fall off the cliff after a few minutes.

definition: A device deliberately slowing down to avoid overheating.
example: An NVMe drive without a heatsink can thermally throttle during a long copy.

definition: Storage Networking Industry Association, which publishes storage standards including the Solid State Storage Performance Test Specification for measuring steady-state SSD performance.
example: SNIA's test specification preconditions a drive before measuring.

definition: Terabytes written: an SSD's endurance rating, the total host writes the warranty covers.
example: A 1 TB drive at 0.3 DWPD for 5 years is rated about 547.5 TBW.

definition: Drive writes per day: an endurance rating saying how many times the drive's full capacity may be written each day for the warranty period.
example: 1 DWPD on a 2 TB drive means 2 TB of writes per day.

definition: Serial ATA, the common interface for desktop hard disks and SSDs, with a 6 Gb/s link (about 600 MB/s of data) and AHCI's single command queue.
example: A SATA SSD tops out near 550 MB/s however fast its flash is.

definition: Serial Attached SCSI, the enterprise drive interface used for high-end hard disks and SSDs.
example: 15,000 rpm SAS drives were the fastest spinning disks.

definition: Advanced Host Controller Interface, the standard way SATA controllers talk to the host: one command list per port with up to 32 outstanding commands.
example: AHCI's 32-command limit caps throughput at 400,000 IOPS for 80 µs requests.

definition: PCI Express, the high-speed serial bus connecting expansion cards and NVMe SSDs to the CPU, built from lanes whose speed depends on the generation.
example: A PCIe 4.0 ×4 link carries about 8 GB/s.

definition: The paired ring buffers NVMe (and io_uring) use: the host places commands in a submission queue and the device posts results to a completion queue, often one pair per CPU core.
example: Core 2 submits on SQ2 and reaps results from CQ2.

definition: A device register the host writes to tell an NVMe controller that new commands are waiting in a submission queue.
example: Writing the SQ0 tail doorbell tells the SSD to fetch new commands.

definition: Linux's multi-queue block layer, which gives each CPU its own software queue and maps them onto the device's hardware queues to avoid lock contention.
example: NVMe drivers on Linux use blk-mq.

definition: Redundant array of independent disks: combining several drives into one volume for capacity, speed, survival of disk failures, or all three.
example: Six 4 TB disks in RAID 5 give 20 TB usable.

definition: Striping data across disks with no redundancy: capacity and speed add up, but losing any one disk loses the volume.
example: Four disks in RAID 0 are about four times as likely to fail as one.

definition: Mirroring: every disk holds a full copy of the data, so the array survives all but one disk failing, at the cost of capacity.
example: Two 4 TB disks in RAID 1 give 4 TB usable.

definition: A stripe across mirrored pairs: half the raw capacity, and it survives one failure per mirror pair; small writes cost 2 disk I/Os.
example: Eight disks in RAID 10 give four disks' capacity.

definition: Striping with one rotating parity chunk per stripe: one disk's capacity goes to parity, and the array survives any single disk failure. A small write costs 4 disk I/Os.
example: Six 4 TB disks in RAID 5 give 20 TB usable.

definition: Striping with two independent parity chunks (P and Q) per stripe: two disks' capacity goes to parity and the array survives any two failures. A small write costs 6 disk I/Os.
example: Twelve disks in RAID 6 give ten disks' capacity.

definition: One row of chunks across all the disks of an array: the data chunks plus their parity. The stripe unit (or chunk) is the amount written to one disk before moving to the next, often 64–512 KiB.
example: A full-stripe write computes parity from new data alone, avoiding reads.

definition: Redundant data computed from other data, in RAID 5 the XOR of a stripe's data chunks, from which any one missing chunk can be rebuilt.
example: If D1 is lost, XORing D0, D2 and the parity gives it back.

definition: In RAID 6, a parity-like value; P is plain XOR parity and Q is a second, independent Reed–Solomon-style syndrome, so any two missing chunks can be solved for.
example: RAID 6 updates both P and Q on every small write.

definition: A family of error-correcting codes that compute m parity symbols from k data symbols so any m missing symbols can be rebuilt. RAID 6 and HDFS's RS-6-3 erasure coding (6 data, 3 parity cells) use them.
example: RS-6-3 survives any three of nine cells being lost.

definition: The extra disk I/Os a parity array needs for a write smaller than a stripe: RAID 5 reads old data and parity then writes both (4 I/Os); RAID 6 needs 6.
example: Random writes on an 8-disk RAID 5 deliver only a quarter of the raw IOPS.

definition: The risk that a crash after writing new data but before writing its parity leaves a stripe's parity wrong without any record, so a later rebuild produces garbage.
example: md's partial parity log closes the RAID 5 write hole.

definition: Linux's software RAID driver (multiple devices), managed with the mdadm tool.
example: mdadm --create /dev/md0 --level=5 builds a software RAID 5.

definition: Linux's Logical Volume Manager, which pools disks into volume groups and carves out resizable logical volumes; it can also do RAID.
example: LVM lets you grow /home by adding a new disk to its volume group.

definition: md's partial parity log and write journal: two ways of recording enough about in-flight stripe updates to repair parity after a crash, closing the write hole.
example: With PPL enabled, an md RAID 5 can fix inconsistent stripes after a power cut.

definition: A RAID controller's write cache protected by a battery or flash so its contents survive power loss and can be completed afterwards.
example: A battery-backed controller cache finishes interrupted parity updates when power returns.

definition: ZFS's parity RAID (single, double or triple parity as RAID-Z, Z2, Z3). It uses variable-width stripes and copy-on-write, so stripes are never updated in place and there is no write hole.
example: A six-disk raidz2 vdev survives any two disk failures.

definition: Reconstructing a failed disk's contents onto a replacement from the surviving disks' data and parity. The array has reduced or no redundancy until it finishes.
example: Rebuilding a 16 TB member at 150 MB/s takes about 30 hours.

definition: Unrecoverable read error: a sector the drive cannot read back correctly despite its error correction. Datasheets quote limits such as 1 per 10^14 or 10^15 bits read.
example: A URE during a RAID 5 rebuild can leave a stripe unrecoverable.

definition: A probability model for events that happen independently at a constant average rate. With λ events expected, the chance of none is e^−λ.
example: Expecting 3.84 errors, the Poisson chance of none is about 2%.

definition: Storing data as data pieces plus computed parity pieces, so lost pieces can be rebuilt; it gives replication-like protection with less overhead.
example: HDFS RS-6-3 erasure coding stores 1.5× the data instead of 3×.

definition: An open-source distributed storage system providing object, block and file storage across many machines, replicating or erasure-coding data between them.
example: Ceph spreads each object's replicas across different hosts.

definition: A separate copy of data from which it can be restored after deletion, corruption or disaster. RAID is not a backup, because it faithfully mirrors deletions and corruption.
example: A nightly backup to another site survives an accidental rm -rf; RAID doesn't.

definition: Malicious software that encrypts a victim's files and demands payment for the key.
example: Ransomware encrypting a RAID array's files encrypts every mirror too.

definition: Failures that are not independent, because devices share an environment, age, batch, firmware or workload, making several fail close together more likely than chance predicts.
example: Disks from one batch in one hot chassis can fail within days of each other.

definition: A cloud-backup company that publishes quarterly failure statistics for the hundreds of thousands of drives it runs.
example: Backblaze's data shows failure rates vary widely between drive models.

definition: A copy-on-write file system and volume manager from Sun (2005) that merges RAID, volume management and the file system, with checksums on every block, snapshots and its own ARC cache.
example: A ZFS pool can detect and repair a corrupted block from a mirror copy.

definition: The open-source project that maintains ZFS for Linux, FreeBSD and other systems. On Linux it ships as a separate kernel module.
example: Ubuntu packages OpenZFS as zfsutils-linux.

definition: The workstation and server company (acquired by Oracle in 2010) that created NFS (1984) and ZFS (2005).
example: NFS came out of Sun in 1984.

definition: Silicon Graphics, the workstation company that designed the XFS file system in the 1990s for large files and parallel I/O.
example: SGI released XFS in 1994 for its IRIX operating system.

definition: An independent region of an XFS file system with its own free-space and inode B+ trees, so many threads can allocate in parallel without a global lock.
example: A 4 TB XFS file system might have 4 allocation groups of 1 TB.

definition: The tool that resizes a mounted XFS file system. Growth is routine; shrinking is limited to the last allocation group with restrictions.
example: xfs_growfs /data grows the file system to fill an enlarged volume.

definition: The tool that grows or shrinks ext2/3/4 file systems; growing can be online, shrinking needs the file system unmounted.
example: resize2fs /dev/sdb1 20G shrinks an unmounted ext4 file system to 20 GiB.

definition: A copy that shares the original's extents on disk until one of them is modified, so copying a huge file is nearly instant and takes no extra space at first.
example: cp --reflink=always vm.img vm2.img on XFS or Btrfs completes in moments.

definition: A Btrfs directory tree that can be mounted, snapshotted and managed independently within one file system.
example: / and /home can be separate Btrfs subvolumes on the same partition.

definition: A Linux distribution that uses Btrfs snapshots (via its snapper tool) to roll back failed system upgrades.
example: openSUSE takes a snapshot before every zypper upgrade.

definition: Compressing file data automatically as it is written and decompressing it on read, trading CPU work for less storage I/O. zstd, lzo, zlib and lz4 are common algorithms.
example: Btrfs with zstd compression can store text logs in a fraction of their size.

definition: Btrfs and ZFS features that serialise the difference between two snapshots into a stream, used for efficient incremental backups to another machine.
example: btrfs send -p old new | ssh backup btrfs receive /backups sends only changes.

definition: In Btrfs, the scheme (such as single, DUP, RAID1, RAID10, RAID5/6) used to store data and metadata across devices.
example: Btrfs is often run with the RAID1 profile for metadata and data.

definition: A ZFS storage pool: one or more vdevs whose combined space is shared by all the pool's datasets. The zpool command manages it.
example: zpool create tank raidz2 sda sdb sdc sdd sde sdf makes a pool called tank.

definition: A ZFS virtual device: a disk, mirror or RAID-Z group that the pool stripes data across, or a special-purpose device such as a SLOG.
example: A pool of two six-disk raidz2 vdevs stripes across both.

definition: A ZFS file system (or volume) inside a pool, with its own properties such as compression, record size and sync behaviour.
example: tank/db and tank/home are separate datasets with different settings.

definition: Reading all allocated data in a pool or array and verifying it against checksums or parity, repairing what it can from redundant copies.
example: A monthly zpool scrub finds latent bad sectors before a disk fails.

definition: Adaptive replacement cache: ZFS's own in-memory cache, separate from the Linux page cache, which balances recently used and frequently used blocks to resist being flushed by scans.
example: On a ZFS server, most free RAM ends up in the ARC.

definition: Level-2 ARC: an optional SSD that extends ZFS's read cache beyond RAM. It does not speed up synchronous writes.
example: An L2ARC SSD can hold blocks evicted from the in-memory ARC.

definition: Separate log device: a fast, durable device (usually a power-loss-protected SSD, often mirrored) that holds the ZFS intent log so synchronous writes commit faster.
example: Adding a mirrored SLOG can cut NFS sync-write latency on an HDD pool.

definition: A write that must be durable before it is acknowledged, such as one followed by fsync, an NFS commit or a database log flush.
example: Databases issue synchronous writes for every transaction commit.

definition: A ZFS dataset setting that acknowledges synchronous writes without making them durable, so a crash can lose data the application believes is safe.
example: sync=disabled makes fsync return instantly but breaks durability.

definition: Storing identical blocks only once, tracked in a deduplication table. It saves space only for duplicate data and costs memory, CPU and I/O.
example: ZFS dedup on VM images that share an OS can save a lot of space.

definition: The ZFS dataset property setting the maximum block size for files, often tuned to match a database's page size.
example: A PostgreSQL dataset might use recordsize=8K or 16K after testing.

definition: ZFS's batch of changes committed together every few seconds, written copy-on-write and ending with a new uberblock.
example: Data logged in the ZIL is written to the main pool in the next transaction group.

definition: Log-structured file system: Rosenblum and Ousterhout's early-1990s design that buffers all changes and writes them sequentially as large segments at the end of a log, never overwriting in place.
example: LFS turns many small random writes into one sequential segment write.

definition: Organised like an append-only log: updates are written as new records at the end rather than in place, with a separate step to reclaim old versions.
example: An SSD's FTL is log-structured internally.

definition: A large unit (hundreds of KiB to a few MiB) of an LFS log, written sequentially in one go. Each has a summary block recording which inode and offset each of its blocks belongs to.
example: LFS gathers 1 MiB of changes in memory, then writes one segment.

definition: In LFS, the table from inode number to the inode's current disk address, needed because inodes move every time they are rewritten. It is itself written into the log in pieces.
example: To read inode 42, LFS looks up its latest location in the inode map.

definition: The LFS process that reads partly-dead segments, rewrites their live blocks into a new segment and frees the old ones. Cleaning segments that are mostly live is expensive.
example: Cleaning segments that are 80% live costs 5 segment writes per segment of new data.

definition: LFS's policy for choosing which segments to clean, weighing the space freed and how long it is likely to stay free (segment age) against the cost of copying live data.
example: Cost-benefit cleaning prefers old, cold segments even if they are fuller.

definition: Flash-Friendly File System, Samsung's log-structured Linux file system (merged in Linux 3.8) designed for flash. It separates hot and cold data and uses a node address table to avoid the wandering-tree problem.
example: Many Android phones format their data partition with F2FS.

definition: Hot data changes often; cold data rarely changes. Keeping them apart means cleaned segments or flash blocks are either mostly dead or mostly stable, which cuts copying.
example: F2FS writes hot directory data and cold multimedia to different logs.

definition: F2FS's table mapping node IDs to block addresses, so moving one block updates a table entry instead of rewriting every parent block up to the root.
example: Updating a file's data in F2FS changes one node and its NAT entry.

definition: In log-structured and copy-on-write designs, moving one block forces its parent to be rewritten, then the grandparent, and so on up to the root.
example: Without a node address table, one data update in a log-structured file system rewrites a chain of index blocks.

definition: Write Anywhere File Layout, NetApp's copy-on-write file system for its storage appliances, known for cheap snapshots.
example: WAFL never overwrites live blocks in place.

definition: A storage company whose appliances run the WAFL file system.
example: NetApp filers serve NFS from WAFL.

definition: An embedded key-value store from Meta, based on an LSM tree.
example: Many databases use RocksDB as their storage engine.

definition: A distributed wide-column NoSQL database that stores data in LSM-tree-style sorted files.
example: Cassandra writes go to a commit log and an in-memory table, later flushed to sorted files.

definition: Google's embedded key-value store and the original basis for RocksDB, built on an LSM tree.
example: LevelDB stores data in levels of sorted string tables.

definition: A database that stores values under unique keys with get and put operations, without tables or a query language.
example: Redis and RocksDB are key-value stores.

definition: A directory an NFS server makes available for clients to mount.
example: /srv/home is exported to the cluster's compute nodes.

definition: The well-known network port number for NFS.
example: Firewalls must allow TCP port 2049 for NFSv4.

definition: A server that keeps no per-client session state between requests, so every request carries all it needs. NFSv3's core protocol was designed this way to simplify crash recovery.
example: An NFSv3 READ carries the file handle, offset and count.

definition: A server's record of which clients have which files open, with what modes and locks. NFSv3 avoids it in its core protocol; NFSv4 adds it with OPEN and CLOSE.
example: NFSv4 servers track open-file state per client, protected by leases.

definition: An opaque token an NFS server gives clients to identify a file, typically encoding the file system, inode number and a generation number.
example: READ(fh, offset=8192, count=4096) names the file only by its handle.

definition: A counter stored with an inode and bumped when the inode number is reused, so an old NFS file handle for a deleted file can't accidentally open a new file.
example: A handle with generation 7 is stale once the inode is reused at generation 8.

definition: An operation whose effect or reply differs when repeated. Retrying it after a lost reply can give a misleading result, as when a repeated REMOVE reports 'no such file'.
example: Removing a name is non-idempotent; reading a fixed byte range of an unchanged file is idempotent.

definition: The default NFS mount behaviour: a timed-out request is retried indefinitely, so applications hang rather than see errors while the server is down.
example: A hard-mounted home directory freezes programs until the server returns.

definition: An NFS mount option where a request gives up after a number of retries and returns an error, which nfs(5) warns can cause silent data corruption.
example: A soft mount returns EIO after its retries are exhausted.

definition: NFS protocol operations: READ reads a byte range from a file handle, REMOVE deletes a name from a directory, and CREATE makes a file (EXCLUSIVE CREATE uses a verifier so retransmissions are recognised).
example: REMOVE(dirfh, "tmp.lock") deletes tmp.lock from the directory dirfh names.

definition: A server-side cache of recent requests and their replies, so a retransmitted request gets the original reply instead of being executed twice.
example: A duplicate request cache replays REMOVE's success instead of returning ENOENT.

definition: NFS's guarantee that when one client closes (or fsyncs) a file and another opens it afterwards, the second sees the first's changes. Between those points there are no promises.
example: A writes and closes status.txt; B's later open revalidates and reads the new data.

definition: An NFS client's cache of file attributes such as size and modification time, kept for 3–60 seconds by default (acregmin/acregmax), so ls can show slightly stale sizes.
example: ls on one client may not see another client's append for up to a minute.

definition: An NFSv4 file attribute that changes whenever the file is modified, letting clients detect changes more reliably than with timestamps.
example: A client compares the change attribute on open to decide whether its cache is stale.

definition: A Unix call for advisory whole-file locks; lock files are a convention of creating a file to claim a resource. Both behave differently, or unreliably, over NFS.
example: Two NFS clients using a lock file can both believe they hold it.

definition: Network Lock Manager: the separate protocol NFSv3 uses for file locking; NFSv4 builds locking into the main protocol.
example: NFSv3 fcntl locks go through NLM to the server's lockd.

definition: A small embedded SQL database stored in a single file. Its documentation warns against putting the file on NFS because locking is unreliable there.
example: Mobile apps commonly keep their data in SQLite.

definition: Request for Comments: the numbered documents that specify Internet protocols. NFSv4 is RFC 7530 (replacing RFC 3530); NFSv3 is RFC 1813.
example: RFC 7530 defines NFSv4's OPEN, CLOSE and lease rules.

definition: A time-limited grant from a server: the client must renew it within the lease period or the server reclaims its state, such as open files and locks.
example: An NFSv4 client renews its lease every few tens of seconds.

aliases: grace period after a server reboot
definition: A window after an NFSv4 server reboots during which clients may reclaim the locks and opens they held, before new ones are granted.
example: On a Linux NFS server the grace period defaults to 90 seconds, during which it only accepts reclaim requests for opens and locks.

definition: An NFSv4 request bundling several operations into one round trip.
example: Opening a file can be one COMPOUND of PUTFH, OPEN and GETATTR.

definition: An NFSv4 grant letting a client cache a file aggressively, acting on it locally until the server recalls the delegation because another client wants it.
example: A client with a write delegation can buffer writes without asking the server.

definition: An NFSv4.1 feature giving each client channel numbered slots with a reply cache, so retransmitted requests are recognised and answered without re-executing them.
example: NFSv4.1 sessions make REMOVE retries safe within the slot rules.

definition: Parallel NFS, part of NFSv4.1: the server tells clients where file data lives so they read and write directly to storage nodes in parallel.
example: pNFS lets a client stream a file from several storage servers at once.

definition: The Google File System (2003): a distributed file system for huge, mostly appended files on thousands of cheap machines, with one master for metadata and chunkservers storing 64 MiB chunks in triplicate.
example: GFS stored Google's web crawls.

definition: Hadoop Distributed File System: an open-source system inspired by GFS, with a NameNode holding metadata and DataNodes storing large replicated blocks (commonly 128 MiB).
example: A 1 TiB file in HDFS is 8,192 blocks of 128 MiB.

definition: Apache's open-source framework for distributed storage (HDFS) and processing of very large data sets.
example: Hadoop 3 added erasure coding to HDFS.

definition: HDFS's master server, holding the file system namespace and file-to-block mappings in memory and tracking which DataNodes hold each block.
example: Clients ask the NameNode where blocks are, then read from DataNodes.

definition: An HDFS storage server that holds blocks on local disks, serves them to clients and reports to the NameNode with heartbeats.
example: A block with replication 3 lives on three DataNodes.

definition: A GFS storage server holding 64 MiB chunks; the GFS equivalent of an HDFS DataNode.
example: Each GFS chunk is stored on three chunkservers.

definition: The single coordinating server in GFS (and, as the NameNode, in HDFS) that holds all metadata in memory; file data never flows through it.
example: The GFS master tells a client which chunkservers hold chunk 7.

definition: GFS's unit of file storage, 64 MiB in the paper, each replicated on several chunkservers.
example: A 1 GiB GFS file is 16 chunks of 64 MiB.

definition: How many copies of each block a distributed store keeps; HDFS defaults to 3.
example: With replication factor 3, 600 TB of data uses 1,800 TB of disk.

definition: The tree of file and directory names in a file system. HDFS's NameNode holds its namespace in memory; federation splits it across NameNodes.
example: Creating /logs/2026/10 changes the HDFS namespace.

definition: HDFS's log of namespace changes, persisted by the NameNode and periodically merged into a checkpoint image.
example: Every file creation in HDFS is recorded in the edit log.

definition: HDFS's way of writing replicas: the client sends data to the first DataNode, which forwards it to the second, which forwards it to the third, with acknowledgements flowing back.
example: Writing a block with replication 3 uses a three-node pipeline.

definition: A cabinet of servers that typically share a network switch and power feed, so they can fail together. Rack-aware placement spreads replicas across racks.
example: HDFS puts two replicas on one remote rack and one on the writer's rack.

definition: A periodic message a node sends to show it is alive; missing heartbeats make the master treat it as failed.
example: DataNodes send heartbeats every 3 seconds by default.

definition: GFS's operation for concurrent appends: GFS chooses the offset and writes each record atomically at least once, so readers may see duplicates and padding.
example: Many clients can record-append log entries to one GFS file at once.

definition: A delivery or write guarantee that the operation happens one or more times, so duplicates are possible and readers must deduplicate.
example: GFS record append is at-least-once, so records need unique IDs.

definition: In GFS, the chunkserver holding a lease from the master for a chunk; it chooses the order and offsets of mutations and its secondaries follow.
example: The primary assigns each record-append its offset.

definition: The HDFS limitation that every file and block costs NameNode memory, so millions of small files exhaust its heap even when total data is modest.
example: 100 million one-block files need roughly 30 GB of NameNode heap in a 150-byte-per-object model.

definition: The memory area where a Java virtual machine (JVM) allocates objects. The HDFS NameNode keeps its whole namespace on the JVM heap.
example: A NameNode might run with a 64 GB heap.

definition: A component whose failure stops the whole system.
example: Early HDFS's lone NameNode was a single point of failure.

definition: An HDFS daemon that stores the shared edit log for high-availability NameNodes; a quorum of them must accept each edit.
example: Three JournalNodes let an active and standby NameNode share edits.

definition: Apache's coordination service, used by HDFS to elect the active NameNode and trigger automatic failover.
example: ZooKeeper detects the active NameNode's failure and promotes the standby.

definition: Switching service from a failed component to a standby one, ideally automatically.
example: HDFS failover promotes the standby NameNode within seconds.

definition: Splitting the HDFS namespace across several independent NameNodes that share the same DataNodes.
example: /user and /data can be served by different NameNodes under federation.

definition: One unit of an erasure-coded stripe: RS-6-3 has 6 data cells and 3 parity cells, any 6 of which can rebuild the stripe.
example: Losing three cells of an RS-6-3 stripe is still recoverable.

definition: HDFS output-stream calls: hflush makes written data visible to new readers; hsync also asks DataNodes to persist it to disk. Striped erasure-coded files don't support them in the ordinary way.
example: A write-ahead log kept on HDFS calls hflush or hsync after each batch of edits.

definition: Storage that keeps whole objects under keys in buckets, accessed over HTTP APIs rather than as a POSIX file system.
example: S3 and Google Cloud Storage are object stores.

definition: Google Cloud's object store. Buckets with hierarchical namespace enabled support real folders, including folder rename.
example: Renaming a folder in a hierarchical-namespace bucket is one operation.

definition: A Google Cloud Storage bucket option that stores folders as real directory entries instead of treating '/' in object names as a naming convention, so folders can be renamed or listed as one operation.
example: Renaming a folder in a hierarchical-namespace bucket is a single folder rename, not a copy of every object under the prefix.
